headline: DEA must answer stay request by 23 November as 4 more firms sue
dek: Four Pennsylvania medical cannabis firms joined the D.C. Circuit challenge on 19 November; a three-judge panel gave the government until 23 November.
key_points: Four vertically integrated Pennsylvania operators filed a second case, No. 26-1325, on 19 November, and the D.C. Circuit clerk consolidated it with the first, No. 26-1324, the same day.
A special panel of Judges Rao, Walker and Garcia ordered the government to respond to the first stay motion by 4 p.m. on 23 November, with any reply due by 4 p.m. on 24 November.
The Pennsylvania firms say their growing and processing arms are not timely applicants, so from 29 November they could not supply even their own dispensaries.
No stay has been reported. Justice Department lawyers told the Pennsylvania firms' counsel on 19 November that the government opposes one, according to WeedPress.
body: The court fight over the DEA's 29 November supply-chain deadline has doubled in size and now has a timetable. Four Pennsylvania medical cannabis companies filed their own challenge at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Thursday 19 November. The clerk consolidated it that day with the case brought a day earlier by operators in Utah, Arizona and Oklahoma, the court's docket shows.

Hours later, a special panel of three judges ordered the government to respond to the first emergency stay motion by 4 p.m. Eastern on Monday 23 November. Any reply from the companies is due by 4 p.m. on Tuesday 24 November. That leaves the court five days to act before the deadline, which falls on the Sunday after Thanksgiving. As of 20 November no outlet we read had reported a stay.
## Who the new petitioners are

The second case is No. 26-1325. The petitioners are G.P.M.II, LLC, MLH Explorations LLC, Tri-Mountain Pure, LLC and Story of PA CR, LLC, according to the docket for the lead case, No. 26-1324, Standard Wellness Utah, LLC v. DEA. Beth C. Neitzel of Foley Hoag entered an appearance for them on 19 November and filed an emergency motion to stay the DEA's action the same evening, with five supporting declarations.

Each of the four holds a Pennsylvania Department of Health grower/processor licence and at least one dispensary licence, according to WeedPress, which has read the motion. Together they say they supply their own stores and more than 100 other licensed Pennsylvania dispensaries, and serve tens of thousands of patients a month. Kind Green Buds reports that G.P.M.II is associated with the multistate operator INSA and that Story of PA CR is affiliated with Ascend Wellness Holdings.

That takes the challenge to seven companies in four states. As we reported on 20 November, the first three are Standard Wellness Utah, Verde Americano of Arizona and NW Confections OK of Oklahoma. The Pennsylvania filing adds a large, limited-licence state with a vertically integrated market, which none of the first three represents.
## A different problem: the form that came too late

The first petitioners' complaint is about trading partners who missed the federal window. The Pennsylvania companies' complaint is about themselves. They say they applied between 28 April and 26 June to register their dispensaries, but did not apply for their manufacturing operations. The reason they give, as relayed by WeedPress, is that DEA field agents and help-line staff told manufacturers to wait for a form specific to medical marijuana, and that form was not available before the window closed.

Court records filed with the first stay motion make a related claim, according to the same outlet: the DEA did not open a dedicated manufacturer or distributor application until 5 October, more than three months after the window shut, and its distributor form offered no medical marijuana drug code. These are the companies' allegations. The government has not yet answered them in court.

The consequence, if the companies are right about how the guidance works, is stark. Their dispensaries are timely applicants. Their grow and processing sites are not. Under the DEA's 30 October notice, timely applicants may deal only with other timely applicants and registrants from 29 November. A company in that position could not move product from its own facility to its own shop.
> The first lawsuit said the deadline cuts companies off from their neighbours. The second says it cuts them off from themselves.
## What they are asking for

The Pennsylvania companies ask the court to stay what they call the counterparty restriction, which they locate in paragraphs 5 to 8 and 11 of the DEA's notice, WeedPress reports. Their legal claims track the first case: that the notice is a legislative rule issued without notice and comment, that it conflicts with 21 C.F.R. 1301.13, and that it is arbitrary and capricious.

On harm, they say their manufacturing arms stand to lose hundreds of thousands of dollars a month from sales to third-party dispensaries alone, and that they would have to close facilities and lay off workers. They say they asked the DEA on 12 November to stay the deadline and had no answer by 17 November. Justice Department lawyers told their counsel on 19 November that the government opposes a stay, according to WeedPress.
## What the court has done so far

The docket shows the sequence. The first petition and emergency motion were filed on 18 November. On 19 November the clerk set routine dates for initial filings, running to 21 December and 4 January 2027, then consolidated the two cases. Government lawyers J. Kain Day and Daniel Aguilar entered appearances for the DEA, its administrator Terrance Cole and, in the second case, the Justice Department and Todd Blanche. The per curiam order setting the 23 and 24 November dates was entered at 4:27 p.m.

Two cautions. First, the briefing order refers to the first stay motion; the docket entry we read does not set a separate date for the Pennsylvania motion, which was filed about two hours later. Second, the docket lists a further per curiam order from the special panel on 20 November, but the entry carried no description when we checked and we have not seen its text. We are not characterising it.

A fast briefing schedule is not a stay. As the law firm Bradley notes in an analysis published on 20 November, filing a petition does not suspend an agency action, and an administrative stay is a short pause that lets a court consider an emergency request without ruling on the merits. The same analysis flags the question that matters to everyone outside the case: whether any order would protect only the petitioners or reach all timely applicants.
## Regulators say they are still in the dark

The pressure is not only in court. Gillian Schauer, executive director of the Cannabis Regulators Association, told a webinar on Friday 20 November that DEA headquarters has not met regulators or answered basic questions, such as how states with both medical and adult-use licences fit in, The Washington Times reports. She said she does not speak for all regulators.

Schauer warned that patients in some states could find dispensaries short of product, or shut. She added that some states report all of their testing laboratories are seeking DEA registration, which could leave none to test state-regulated product. The webinar was hosted by the Coalition for Cannabis Scheduling Reform. Shane Pennington of Blank Rome, who is on the coalition's legal team and is challenging the guidance at the D.C. Circuit, argued there that the DEA changed the rules by email without public comment.
## What it means for operators

Nothing has changed on the ground. The 29 November date stands unless the court or the DEA moves it, and the DEA's notice says trading with ineligible partners can be grounds to deny an application or revoke a registration. Bradley's analysis also points out that the notice lets timely dispenser and distributor applicants keep handling certain inventory acquired before 30 October, including stock from partners outside the eligible groups. That is a carve-out for existing stock, not for new purchases.

For vertically integrated operators in other states, the Pennsylvania filing is a prompt to check each licence separately. On the companies' account, a group can be a timely applicant at the counter and a non-applicant at the grow. We cannot say how many businesses are in that position; no source we read gave a count.
## What to watch

On 23 November at 4 p.m. Eastern the government's response is due. It will be the DEA's first full public defence of the notice. On 24 November the companies' reply is due. On 25 November the first petitioners' requested decision date arrives. On 29 November the deadline takes effect unless something changes. Watch also for the text of the 20 November order, and for whether more operators or any state join the case.
